works.abstract: Microplastic spectral analysis is one of the most time-consuming processes in studying microplastic pollution, often requiring days per sample. Researchers are transitioning to automated batch and hyperspectral image analysis techniques to enhance efficiency. Open Specy, initially aimed at manual single-spectrum analysis, has now integrated automated methods. This updated version, Open Specy 1.0, introduces several new features, including two algorithms for automated processing (smoothing and particle compression), an extensive library containing over 40,000 open-source Raman and FTIR spectra, and two machine learning classifiers (logistic regression and k medoids) developed from this library. Furthermore, it includes a revamped user interface, an R package, and a benchmark data set for testing future advancements in automated techniques. Researchers evaluated various configurations for hyperspectral smoothing, particle identification, compression, and splitting, to achieve combined recovery rates between 50 and 150% particle counts, identities, and sizes with a coefficient of variation (CV) of less than 40% (the accredited standard). Mean absorbance times the standard deviation provided a consistent particle identification. Hyperspectral smoothing led to a 96% combined recovery rate and reduced variability (CV = 38%) compared to the 86% recovery (CV = 83%) of nonsmoothed controls. Additionally, compressing spectra for particles was significantly faster (>3×) and showed similar accuracy but with reduced variability than processing each pixel individually. Key challenges persist in automating spectral analysis, particularly in refining particle splitting algorithms, and improving identification routines to minimize false positives and negatives. New methods in sample preparation for better stabilization and dispersion of particles could overcome some of these issues.
works.title: Open Specy 1.0: Automated (Hyper)spectroscopy for Microplastics

works.abstract: Plastic pollution is a major global issue due to its pervasiveness in marine ecosystems. Microplastics (MPs; plastic < 5mm in size) are ubiquitous and persistent within these environments and can enter marine organisms via three primary exposure routes - ingestion (direct and indirect), inhalation, and dermal contact. While the presence of MPs in the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, gills, and skin as a result of these routes is well documented, movement of MPs to other organs and tissues following uptake - known as translocation - remains poorly understood, particularly in marine vertebrates (fish, pinnipeds, cetaceans, elasmobranchs, seabirds, and sea turtles). Here we conducted a systematic review of scientific literature to understand which taxa and organ systems MP translocation occurs in and to identify knowledge gaps and future directions. We use the term "putative translocation" to recognise that detection of MPs in distal tissues or organs does not necessarily demonstrate movement of particles between compartments, but may provide evidence consistent with translocation. Across 89 peer-reviewed studies identified, putative MP translocation was suggested in all six marine vertebrate taxa, with the majority (93%; n = 83) focussing on fish. MPs were detected across a range of organ systems, occurring most frequently in the hearts and spleens of fish, blubber of pinnipeds, acoustic fats of cetaceans, reproductive organs of elasmobranchs, and muscles of seabirds. In sea turtles, MPs were detected in all analysed organs (subcutaneous fat, heart, kidney, liver, muscle, reproductive organs, and spleen). Several knowledge gaps were identified, such as understanding the mechanisms and health impacts of MP translocation. Additionally, a lack of methodological standardisation in sample processing, contamination control, and reporting across the studies was detected. A guideline of best practices is provided to facilitate harmonisation across future studies to better understand the extent of MP translocation and the potential health risks posed.
works.title: Exploring the occurrence of microplastic translocation in marine vertebrates with guidelines for harmonisation
